title: What are the Big Four, and how is their consulting different from MBB?
description: Deloitte, PwC, EY and KPMG explained: their size, their strategy arms, the kind of consulting work they do and how it compares with MBB.
hook: The Big Four are Deloitte, PwC, EY and KPMG: professional services firms that began in audit and accounting and now run some of the largest consulting businesses in the world. Compared with MBB, their consulting leans more towards technology, operations, risk and implementation, with longer projects and bigger teams, while each firm's dedicated strategy arm does work much closer to MBB. Here is how they are organised, how the work and interviews differ, and how to target the right part of each firm.
body:
Who they are

All four sell audit, tax, advisory and consulting services through networks of member firms around the world. In fiscal 2025 they earned about $220B between them: Deloitte $70.5B, PwC $56.9B, EY $53.2B and KPMG $39.8B, with roughly 1.5 million people in total. Those figures include audit and tax, so they show scale rather than the size of each consulting practice.

Two features of their structure matter for candidates. First, each country's member firm largely runs its own recruiting, so processes differ between, say, the UK and the US. Second, auditor independence rules limit which non-audit services a firm can sell to companies it audits, which shapes the client mix of its consulting teams.

What their consulting looks like

Big Four consulting is broad. A large share is technology, operations, risk, people and implementation work, often on longer projects with bigger teams. Each firm also has a deals or transactions business and a dedicated strategy arm:

  • Monitor Deloitte, built on Monitor Group, which Deloitte acquired in 2013.
  • Strategy& at PwC, the former Booz & Company, acquired in 2014. It runs its own recruiting.
  • EY-Parthenon, built on The Parthenon Group, acquired in 2014. Since 2025 it also includes EY's wider strategy and transactions teams.
  • KPMG's strategy group.

The strategy arms are where the work, and the interviews, look most like MBB.

How it differs from MBB

DimensionMBBBig Four
Main workStrategy and transformation for senior leadersTechnology, operations, risk and implementation, plus strategy in specialist arms
SizeTens of thousands of peopleHundreds of thousands, across many service lines
ProjectsOften weeks to months, small teamsOften longer, larger teams, more time inside the client
HiringFew places, very selectiveMany more openings at every level
InterviewsIndividual cases and personal experience questionsVaries by role: online tests, video interviews, assessment centres, cases, group exercises

What the interviews look like

Because recruiting runs by country and by business, there is no single Big Four process. Some published examples, as of 2026:

  • Deloitte UK early careers: an online application, an immersive online assessment (behavioural scenarios plus numerical and verbal reasoning), a job simulation with written and recorded video tasks, and a final-stage assessment with a topic discussion and a skills and motivation interview.
  • PwC UK early careers: an online application, an online assessment with a behavioural profile and timed reasoning tests, an on-demand video interview, a virtual assessment centre, and a final in-person interview with a senior leader.
  • EY US says the style, format and number of rounds depend on business needs, and may include prerecorded video, live video and case study interviews.

Strategy arms and experienced-hire roles usually lean much more heavily on case interviews. The firm-by-firm guides cover each: Deloitte, PwC and Strategy&, EY and EY-Parthenon and KPMG.

A typical Big Four case: late orders

Suppose you interview for a supply chain transformation role. The case: a distributor ships 500,000 orders a year and 20% arrive late. Each late order costs about $30 in express shipping and customer credits. (Illustrative numbers.)

  • Late orders: 500,000 × 20% = 100,000 a year.
  • Cost: 100,000 × $30 = $3.0M a year.
  • Segmenting by warehouse, supplier, route and carrier shows that one warehouse accounts for 60% of late orders: 60,000 orders, or 60,000 × $30 = $1.8M.
  • If a new picking process halved that warehouse's late orders, the saving would be $1.8M × 50% = $900k a year.

An MBB-style answer might stop at the recommendation. Because Big Four roles often involve delivery, a strong answer here also covers how to make the change stick:

"Most of the $3M comes from one warehouse, so I'd start there. I'd pilot the new picking process on one shift for four weeks, track on-time rates daily, and train the supervisors on the other shifts before rolling it out. If on-time rates hold, the saving is about $900k a year."

A weaker answer lists every possible cause of lateness without sizing any of them, or recommends new software without asking whether people will use it. Be ready to explain both how you would solve the problem and how you would work with people to deliver the solution.

Which part should you apply to?

Read job titles carefully. "Consulting" at a Big Four firm can mean strategy, technology, risk, operations, deals or human capital, and each has its own interview. Ask yourself which problems you want to work on, check whether the role uses case interviews, and confirm the format with your recruiter. Do not assume one published interview guide describes every country or business unit.

Practice

In the late-orders case, the client says express shipping costs $20 per order and credits average $10. A new carrier would cut express costs to $15. What is the annual saving across all late orders?

Show the answer

The saving is $5 per late order on express shipping ($20 to $15), and credits are unchanged. Across 100,000 late orders: 100,000 × $5 = $500k a year. Worth noting: fixing the warehouse saves more ($900k) and also improves service, so the carrier switch is a complement, not a substitute.

Where to go next

Decide whether to aim for MBB, the Big Four or both, and if group exercises are part of your process, read how group and written cases work.
